question: What is the tapered, inferior termination of the spinal cord called?
explanation: The conus medullaris marks the end of the solid spinal cord, usually situated near the upper lumbar vertebrae. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h1)

question: Why is a lumbar puncture performed in the lower lumbar region of the spine?

options.A: The spinal cord has already terminated, reducing risk of direct injury
options.B: Vertebrae are fused tightly together in the upper back
options.C: The meninges are completely absent below the thoracic vertebrae
options.D: The cerebrospinal fluid pressure is highest in this specific area

explanation: Because the spinal cord ends around the L1 vertebra, needle insertion lower down avoids puncturing neural tissue while safely accessing CSF in the subarachnoid space. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h1)

question: Which meningeal layer is in direct contact with the surface of the spinal cord?
explanation: The pia mater is a delicate membrane that closely adheres to every contour of the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h2)

question: Where is cerebrospinal fluid normally found surrounding the spinal cord?
explanation: The subarachnoid space lies beneath the arachnoid mater and contains the circulating cerebrospinal fluid. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h2)

question: Which structure within the spinal grey matter contains the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons?
explanation: The anterior horns of the grey matter contain motor neurons that send signals directly to skeletal muscles. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h3)

question: What is the primary structural component that gives spinal white matter its distinct appearance and function?
explanation: White matter appears white due to the fatty myelin sheaths surrounding axon bundles traveling up and down the cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h3)

question: Which ascending pathway is primarily responsible for transmitting pain and temperature sensations?
explanation: The spinothalamic tract ascends from the spinal cord to the thalamus, carrying crude touch, pain, and temperature information. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h4)

question: What is a common characteristic of most sensory pathways ascending to the brain?

options.A: They exclusively travel down the anterior funiculus of the white matter
options.B: They bypass the thalamus entirely to reach the cerebellum directly
options.C: They consist of only a single uninterrupted neuron from skin to cerebral cortex
options.D: They typically cross over (decussate) to the opposite side of the central nervous system

explanation: Most sensory and motor pathways cross the midline, meaning one side of the brain processes information from and controls the contralateral side of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h4)

question: Which descending pathway is primarily responsible for conscious, precise, and skilled voluntary movements of the limbs?
explanation: The corticospinal tracts convey motor commands from the motor cortex down to spinal motor neurons for voluntary muscle control. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h5)

question: What is the consequence of damage to the lateral corticospinal tract on the same side of the body below the level of the lesion?

options.A: Uncontrolled hyperactivity of the autonomic nervous system
options.B: Loss of voluntary motor control in the ipsilateral limbs
options.C: Inability to feel pain and temperature on the opposite side
options.D: Complete permanent loss of all sensory perception

explanation: Because fibers in the lateral corticospinal tract have already crossed in the brainstem, damage at the spinal level results in ipsilateral motor deficits. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h5)

question: Where are the cell bodies of sensory neurons entering the spinal cord located?
explanation: The dorsal root ganglion houses the unipolar cell bodies of incoming sensory nerve fibers. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h6)

question: What does a dermatome map represent in clinical neurological assessment?

options.A: The exact pathway taken by motor impulses traveling to a skeletal muscle
options.B: The distribution of blood vessels supplying the spinal cord meninges
options.C: The area of skin innervated by the sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve
options.D: The boundaries between different vertebrae in the spinal column

explanation: Dermatomes map cutaneous sensory supply, allowing clinicians to pinpoint spinal nerve root damage based on where numbness occurs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h6)

question: Which component of a reflex arc is responsible for detecting the initial stimulus?
explanation: Receptors specialize in detecting environmental changes, converting them into electrical signals that trigger the reflex arc. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h7)

question: What is a defining feature of a monosynaptic reflex arc like the knee-jerk reflex?

options.A: It only occurs in the cranial nerves supplying facial muscles
options.B: It requires conscious thought and deliberation by the cerebral cortex
options.C: It contains only a single synapse between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron
options.D: It involves multiple interneurons delaying the response time significantly

explanation: Monosynaptic reflexes feature a direct synapse from sensory to motor neuron without intervening interneurons, making them extremely fast. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h7)

question: What term describes paralysis affecting both legs following a lower thoracic or lumbar spinal cord injury?
explanation: Paraplegia refers to motor and sensory impairment in the lower half of the body, usually resulting from lower spinal cord lesions. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h8)

question: Which clinical phenomenon is characterized by sudden, dangerous hypertension triggered by a distended bladder in a patient with a high spinal cord injury?
explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia is an exaggerated sympathetic reflex response to below-lesion discomfort, most commonly a full bladder or bowel, causing severe hypertension. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T24#GNS211_U3_T24_h8)
